intro: In 70 CE the Roman army destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem. For many Jews, the center of their worship was gone. Rabbinic tradition tells of a teacher who asked Rome for one small town full of scholars. From that town, Yavneh, a new way of Jewish life began to grow, built around study, prayer and argument.

This unit follows that growth over about 500 years. You will meet the Tannaim, whose teachings became the Mishnah. You will meet the Amoraim, who discussed the Mishnah in the Galilee and in Babylonia. You will see how empires, wars and friendships shaped their schools, and how the Talmud keeps both sides of an argument.

By the end, you will be able to place the rabbis on a timeline. You will tell a tanna from an amora and name the great academies. You will also compare what the Talmud tells about its past with what historians can show.
bigQuestion: How did the rabbis build a new center for Jewish life after the Temple fell?

timeline.t: The Maccabean revolt begins against a Syrian Greek king
Pompey enters Jerusalem; Roman rule begins
Hillel and Shammai teach in Jerusalem
Rome destroys the Second Temple; the court at Yavneh grows
The Bar Kokhba revolt; Rabbi Akiva dies
Rabbi Judah the Prince completes the Mishnah, tradition holds
Rav founds the academy at Sura, tradition says
Nehardea is destroyed; scholars move to Pumbedita
Ravina dies; the Babylonian Gemara nears its close
The age of the Geonim begins

words.d: a Second Temple group that held to traditions beyond the written Torah; the rabbis saw them as their forerunners
a Second Temple group tied to the priests that rejected the Pharisees' traditions
the town where, tradition says, rabbis rebuilt Jewish learning after 70 CE
a teacher from the Mishnah era, up to about 220 CE
a teacher of the Gemara era, c. 220–500 CE
the first written collection of rabbinic teaching, c. 200 CE
the Amoraim's discussion of the Mishnah
a teaching of the Tannaim not in the Mishnah
a school where rabbis and students studied together
the leader of Babylonian Jews recognized by the Persian kings
rabbis after the Amoraim, c. 500–600 CE, who finished shaping the Talmud
head of the academy at Sura or Pumbedita, c. 589–1038 CE

test.q: Who does rabbinic tradition say edited the Mishnah c. 200 CE?
test.why: Tradition credits Rabbi Judah the Prince with the Mishnah.

test.q: Which group ruled Judea just before the Maccabean revolt?
test.why: Antiochus IV, a Syrian Greek king, outlawed Jewish practice in 167 BCE.

test.q: When was the Second Temple destroyed?
test.why: Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE.

test.q: According to the Talmud, what did Yochanan ben Zakkai ask of the Roman general?
test.why: Gittin 56b tells that he asked for Yavneh and its sages.

test.q: Which rabbi, the Jerusalem Talmud says, hailed Bar Kokhba as a king-messiah?
test.why: The Jerusalem Talmud, Ta'anit 4, tells that Rabbi Akiva said this, and another rabbi disagreed.

test.q: Which pair founded two famous schools whose debates fill the Mishnah?
test.why: The Houses of Hillel and Shammai argue throughout the Mishnah.

choices: A teacher of the Mishnah era
A head of a Babylonian academy after 589 CE
A teacher of the Gemara era
test.why: Amoraim taught c. 220–500 CE; their discussions became the Gemara.

choices: A teaching of the Tannaim left out of the Mishnah
test.why: The Gemara quotes baraitot as proofs and objections.

test.q: Which city held a great academy in the Land of Israel?
test.why: Tiberias was a center in the Land of Israel; the others were in Babylonia.

test.q: In disputes between Abaye and Rava, the law follows
test.why: Bava Metzia 22b gives this rule, with six cases for Abaye.

test.q: Whom does tradition call "the end of instruction"?
test.why: Bava Metzia 86a says this of Rav Ashi and Ravina.

choices: The Jewish leader of Babylonia recognized by Persian kings
test.why: The Exilarch, Resh Galuta, served under the Sasanian kings.

choices: Heads of the academies of Sura and Pumbedita after the Talmud
test.why: The Geonim led c. 589–1038 CE and answered questions by letter.
Chavruta is paired study, as the story of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish shows.

test.q: Which group, historians say, did not believe in an Oral Torah beyond the written text?
test.why: Josephus and rabbinic sources describe the Sadducees as rejecting the Pharisees' traditions.

write.prompt: How did the rabbis keep Jewish learning alive after the Temple fell? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Gittin 56b (Yochanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh), Bava Metzia 84a (Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish) or Bava Metzia 86a (Rav Ashi and Ravina). Explain what each passage says and how traditional and academic readers have read it.
tips: Name the tractate and page for each passage you cite.
Say who tells each story: "the Talmud says" or "historians date."
Compare what the story teaches with what historians can show, without judging either.
Use the unit's terms: tanna, amora, academy, Exilarch.
